slides.text: In 1966, the Grand Prize for Painting at the Venice Biennale went to a room of mirrors, small motors and moving light.
The artist was Julio Le Parc, born in Argentina in 1928. He had come to Paris in 1958 on a French scholarship.
In 1960 he helped start a group of artists in Paris who signed their work together, as a group, instead of one by one.
They wanted people to take part in the work, not just stand and look at it.
On April 19, 1966, the group spent a day, from 8 a.m. to midnight, taking their pieces into the streets of Paris, among them a giant kaleidoscope.
In 1972, a Paris museum offered him a retrospective. He let a coin toss decide, and the coin said no.
One of his light pieces, first made in 1962, uses motors and projected light to throw moving light across a surface more than four meters tall.
He died in May 2026, at 97, while preparing a show of his work at Tate Modern in London.
It opened that June without him, and it runs until May 3, 2027.
